title: Elm and the Sparkle Sneeze
markdown:
The hills were round and soft, and the sky came down to meet them like a blanket tucked under a chin. Elm lived there. Elm was a young elf with bluebell eyes and quick light fingers, and a smile that could coax a sunbeam even when the clouds were sulking. Elm liked quiet walks, the hush of wind in leaves, and the sort of evening that smelled of honeysuckle and damp earth.

One evening the day tiptoed toward bedtime. The sky went pink, then orange, as if it were putting on its night clothes slowly. Elm wandered into Glowworm Glade. Tiny lights blinked on and off in the grass, like fallen stars that had decided to stay a while. The air felt like a small hug. Near the Bluebell Cliffs, the bell-flowers nodded, deep blue, sleepy, as if they had already heard a lullaby.

Elm passed a mossy rock. A puff of smoke no bigger than a dandelion seed drifted up. It smelled of toasted marshmallows.

Then: ACHOO.

Tiny orange sparks zipped through the air, warm and bright, like fireflies who had forgotten to wait for full dark.

Elm peeked. Behind the rock sat the smallest dragon Elm had ever seen, no bigger than a fluffy rabbit. Scales the colour of a hearth ember. Wings that fluttered like a butterfly exploring a meadow, not like a storm. The dragon blinked honey-coloured eyes.

Elm learned, soon enough, that the dragon was called Flicker.

Flicker sneezed again. ACHOO. A spark landed in a puddle. Pop. Fizz. The puddle bubbled with tiny lights, as if it had been tickled. Elm’s giggle rose up before Elm could stop it. Flicker looked surprised, then sneezed once more. Sparks in soft dark mud. Sizzle-pop. The mud puffed into little brown clouds, then settled, as if it had tried to fly and thought better of it.

“You have a very sparkly sneeze,” Elm said, stepping closer.

Flicker tilted a head. A tiny squeak, half chirp, half jingle of bells. Another sneeze. A spark danced past Elm’s nose and fizzled. Elm did not flinch.

“It’s quite all right,” Elm whispered, palm up. “Are you lost, little one?”

Flicker’s nose wriggled. A puff of smoke. The warm snout nudged Elm’s hand, a tickle like a feather. Elm thought of empty tummies and of being small in a large glade.

“You must be hungry. I know a patch of moon-berries. Would you like to come?”

Flicker chirped and hopped. Soft thuds on moss. Along the way the sneezes kept coming, but Elm pointed each spark as if it were a small surprise, not a problem.

“Look. That one made a dewdrop shine.”

“That one warmed a pebble enough to hold.”

Flicker’s tail, sunset-coloured, began to wag. The sneezes grew smaller. The sparks grew fewer. At the moon-berry bushes the fruit glowed with a quiet inviting light. Flicker nibbled. Sweet juice. A happy hum.

They sat among the berries. Flicker snuggled close. A puff of smoke no bigger than a whisper, smelling of warm cookies. No sparks at all.

Elm did not make a speech about yarn. Elm only sat, and the berries shone, and Flicker’s sneeze had learned the difference between lost and found.

They walked back through the darkening glade. Glowworms blinked, little lanterns along the path. Elm’s home would be warm: a small bed, a window that knew the hills, a saucer of water for a dragon who had been sneezing sparks into puddles only an hour ago. Flicker’s snout stayed warm against a kind palm. Inside, Elm set a cushion by the hearth, not too close to the coals. Flicker curled there, ember scales, sunset tail, honey eyes already sleepy. No sparks. Only a cookie-scented puff, and then the quiet of a glade that had made a friend. The hills tucked the sky in again, and the marshmallow smell lingered, faint as a goodnight.
